article_title: Collective Bargaining and University Governance.
citation: Bloustein, Edward J. (1973). Collective Bargaining and University Governance. Speech presented at the annual meeting of the Association of American Colleges. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED074928
title: University and college presidents should welcome and support the development of strong faculty collective bargaining
description: The article's closing recommendation, drawn from the author's argument that fears of unionism are "grossly overstated" and that bargaining makes power-sharing a matter of right rather than beneficence. On balance, he advises presidents to embrace strong faculty collective bargaining rather than resist it, since agreements with an organized faculty group are preferable to individual bargaining. The recommendation is scoped to his special circumstances: a largely procedural contract covering economic conditions and due process while leaving educational policy to traditional governance structures.
requirements: An essentially procedural contract that leaves faculty selection, appointment, promotion, and educational policy to traditional academic governance structures outside the contract
constraints: Based on one year's experience with one AAUP bargaining unit at Rutgers and a contract the author describes as special in kind
target_learners: university and college presidents and administrators
target_learning_goals: shared governance and power-sharing in academic institutions
fair employment and due-process procedures for faculty
examples: At Rutgers the author reports the senate's authority broadened without AAUP domination, and he prefers negotiating with an organized group representing 2500 faculty to individual agreements with Bennington's 65.
key_sources: Bloustein, Edward J. (1973). Collective Bargaining and University Governance. Speech presented at the annual meeting of the Association of American Colleges. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED074928

article_title: Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Language Proficiency Acquisition, Assessment, and Communicative Behavior, Series B. Teacher Edition. Bilingual Education Teacher Training Packets.
citation: Calderon, Margarita; DiPietro, Robert J.; Larsen-Pusey, Mary Ann; Rubio, Olga. (1982). Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Series B. Teacher Edition. Evaluation, Dissemination and Assessment Center, Dallas. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED226608
title: Open-ended scenario pattern: collaboratively planned dialogues enacted through off-stage, on-stage, and debriefing phases
description: The open-ended scenario is a pedagogical device designed by DiPietro which resembles a role play in that it grows from a set of circumstances, but differs in that dialogues are planned collaboratively by second-language learners and then acted out. It unfolds in phases: an off-stage phase where the scenario is discussed and planned, an on-stage phase where the dialogue is acted out, and a debriefing stage where interactions and transactions are discussed with the language facilitator. The packet's Part 4 provides guidelines for constructing open-ended scenarios and follow-up procedures.
requirements: A language facilitator leads the debriefing stage in which interactions and transactions are discussed
constraints: The packet presents the scenario device as needing guidelines for construction, provided in Part 4
target_learners: second language learners in K-12 and adult classrooms
target_learning_goals: strategic and interactional competence through authentic language use
examples: Part 4 of the packet covers preparation for open-ended scenario development, guidelines for construction, and follow-up, supported by workshop transparencies and guided discussion items
key_sources: Calderon, Margarita; DiPietro, Robert J.; Larsen-Pusey, Mary Ann; Rubio, Olga. (1982). Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Series B. Teacher Edition. Evaluation, Dissemination and Assessment Center, Dallas. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED226608

article_title: Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10.
citation: Rivera, Charlene, Ed. (1984). Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED240882
title: Do not exit students from bilingual programs on face-to-face conversational fluency alone
description: The volume argues that apparent conversational fluency in English is a linguistic facade that can hide large gaps in academically related aspects of proficiency, so exit decisions based on teacher judgements or tests assessing face-to-face skills are likely to set students up for academic difficulty. Because academic proficiency takes considerably longer to develop than surface fluency, exit criteria must rest on a theoretical framework relating language proficiency to academic achievement rather than on intuitive judgements of fluency.
requirements: A theoretical framework relating language proficiency to academic achievement to ground entry/exit criteria
constraints: Relevant empirical studies on threshold levels for effective participation in all-English classrooms remain to be done, per the article
target_learners: Language minority students in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of academic language proficiency for program exit decisions
examples: The article documents students frequently exited from bilingual classrooms on the assumption that fluent face-to-face English means they can survive an all-English classroom
key_sources: Rivera, Charlene, Ed. (1984). Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED240882

article_title: The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual.
citation: Coombs, Lucinda H. (1987). The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual. Maine Dept. of Educational and Cultural Services / University of Maine. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED324536
title: Design writing assignments around topics students care about and can substantively respond to
description: The manual instructs teachers to offer a choice of topics because, as it states, "Unless a writer is interested in the topic, has an opinion about it, and hasthe knowledge to write a substantive response, the writing is not going to be good." Topics should be generally familiar, worth writing about, clearly stated, and require evaluation rather than recitation of facts. Assignments should foster success and be calibrated carefully to avoid overestimating or underestimating student ability.
requirements: Topics must be familiar, clearly stated, and require the same critical thinking skills as the GED essay
constraints: Overestimating ability undermines confidence; underestimating causes frustration and limits progress
examples: The manual ranks the personal narrative as the easiest writing type and suggests starting there before moving students toward the essay
key_sources: Coombs, Lucinda H. (1987). The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual. Maine Dept. of Educational and Cultural Services / University of Maine. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED324536

article_title: Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration.
citation: Willower, Donald J. (1992). Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration. Paper presented at the annual convention of the University Council for Educational Administration, Minneapolis. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED355669
title: Institutionalize reflective methods in organizational norms, symbols, and procedures so critical appraisal becomes routine
description: The paper argues that individual reflective administrators need organizational support, since reflective methods threaten fixed and favorite beliefs and will not take hold without widespread openness to communication and critical assessment of ideas. Institutionalization means embedding reflective methods in the norms, values, symbols, shared meanings, values structures and procedures of the organization, so that critical appraisal becomes routine, part and parcel of everyday organizational life. The paper reports that institutionalized reflective methods should lead to better and more ethical organizational decisions and that decisions subject to reflective assessment are usually easy to defend.
requirements: Organizational arrangements, beliefs, and practices geared toward reflective methods
Widespread openness to communication and to the critical assessment of ideas
constraints: The paper warns reflective methods are not a technology to be imposed, not a panacea nor even a sure thing, and that honest and critical discussions of problems are anything but typical of organizations
examples: The paper lists sample organizational comments such as 'We're not afraid to criticize ideas' and devices for formal groups including a devil's advocate and 'What can go wrong?' sessions
key_sources: Willower, Donald J. (1992). Dewey's Theory of Inquiry and Reflective Administration. Paper presented at the annual convention of the University Council for Educational Administration, Minneapolis. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED355669

article_title: Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993.
citation: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567
title: Goal-oriented framework sequencing EE instructional strategies from ecological foundations through conceptual awareness and investigation skills to environment action skills
description: The newsletter proposes a goal-oriented framework as a basis for organizing instructional strategies for global change education, matching activity types to goal levels. "Agoal-oriented frameworkcould also be used as a basis for organizing instructional strategies." Simulations, models and reading lay the ecological foundations; case-histories, field trips, brainstorming and discussions build conceptual awareness; secondary source investigations, primary data collection, value clarification and moral education develop investigation skills and evaluation of issues; and action workshops, community internship and action analysis projects build environment action skills.
requirements: Instruction must be organized so that activity types match the goal level being targeted, from ecological foundations up to environment action skills
target_learners: school students in global change / environmental education programmes
examples: The article lists simulations, models and reading for ecological foundations; case-histories, field trips, brainstorming sessions and discussions for conceptual awareness; and action workshops, action learning in community internship and action analysis projects for environment action skills
key_sources: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567

article_title: Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993.
citation: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567
title: Infuse global change instruction into existing curricula while ensuring in-depth issue knowledge, investigation skills, citizenship skills and an internal locus of control
description: Because global change instruction is interdisciplinary, the article argues the most effective way to deliver it in schools is to incorporate it into existing curricula rather than teach it as a separate subject. It specifies broad principles the infused curriculum must provide: "An in-depthknowledgeof issues", teaching skills of issue analysis and investigation, teaching citizenship skills for issue remediation, and "An attempt to develop aninternal locus of control". In secondary schools, contents and skills can be integrated into courses such as agriculture, home economics, health, science, social studies or language arts without jeopardising the courses themselves.
requirements: Cooperation from all teachers responsible for the infused programmes, whose willingness to build and carry out an infusion plan the article calls a key component of effectiveness
target_learners: secondary school teachers infusing EE into subject courses
examples: The article states that courses in agriculture, home economics, health, science, social studies or language arts could lend themselves to infusion of global change contents and skills
key_sources: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567

article_title: Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction.
citation: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329
title: Form collaborative learning groups around learners' common interests and goals
description: The guide recommends forming collaborative learning groups by examining intake results, goal setting, and conversations with learners to find shared interests. It advises that "the facilitator or site coordinator can look at common interests among those who are willing to work in groups," giving examples such as parenting skills, job search, and health careers. A shared theme supplies many possible topics for reading, writing, critical reflection, and collective analysis, and groups formed by convenient time or location can instead generate themes in the first weeks of class.
requirements: Initial intake interviews, goal-setting formats, and conversations that surface learners' interests and willingness to work in groups
constraints: Some centers are constrained to hold classes based on a convenient time, day, and location rather than a shared theme
target_learners: Adult literacy and basic education learners
target_learning_goals: Basic academic skills, GED preparation, and employment-related goals
examples: In Scenario 1, a coordinator invites learners interested in health care professions to form a group meeting for three months
key_sources: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329

article_title: Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction.
citation: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329
title: Base initial assessment in real-life contexts using informal, authentic measures alongside standardized testing
description: The guide holds that assessment in collaborative learning should reflect its learner-centered, participatory philosophy. "Assessment is situated in real-life contexts and relevant to what learners already know in their everyday lives," and informal assessment is supportive and focuses on each learner's strengths. Practitioners use authentic reading selections and writing tasks (newspapers, shopping lists, notes) to gauge abilities, and "informal, alternative, and authentic assessment is primarily used in addition to standardized testing."
requirements: Intake interviews, intake forms, authentic reading and writing tasks, and goals and self-assessment formats completed with learners
constraints: Standardized testing may still be required, in which case informal assessment is used in conjunction with it
target_learners: Adult basic education learners entering literacy programs
target_learning_goals: Identifying learner strengths, goals, and instructional needs
examples: The guide adapts its intake and assessment material from Auerbach (1990) and Lyte, et. al. (1986) and provides intake, goal-setting, and action-plan forms in its appendix
key_sources: Philadelphia Mayor's Commission on Literacy. (1994). Collaborative Learning: An Alternative Approach to Adult Literacy Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376329

article_title: Grade One: Math Computation. Case Study #1
citation: Powell, S. R., & Seethaler, P. M. (2007). Grade One: Math Computation (Math Case Study #1). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Peer tutoring as a primary-prevention evidence-based practice in first-grade math
description: At primary prevention, the classroom teacher supplements the district curriculum with a peer-tutoring program run "3 times per week for 30 minutes each session." Each session opens with teacher-led introduction or review, then higher-performing students are paired with lower-performing students to work on the lesson. Topics include number concepts, comparing numbers, addition and subtraction concepts, place value, double-digit addition and subtraction, and missing addends.
requirements: Cross-ability pairing of students, a structured session opening with teacher-led review, and topic materials such as worksheets (e.g., drawing tens and ones for place value)
target_learners: All first-grade students in the general education classroom
target_learning_goals: Number concepts, place value, and addition and subtraction computation
examples: The case study includes a sample peer-tutoring worksheet focusing on place value by asking students to draw tens and ones
key_sources: Powell, S. R., & Seethaler, P. M. (2007). Grade One: Math Computation (Math Case Study #1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED502453

article_title: Pedagogy Is for Kids: Andragogy Is for Adults
citation: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults.
title: Address adult learners' need to know why they should learn something from the beginning of the learning experience
description: The principle holds that facilitators of adult learning should "make the intellectual case for the value of learning in improving the effectiveness of the learner’s performance or the quality of their lives" from the start. The essay argues this is most important for adult learners given the voluntary nature of most adult learning and the many competing demands on adults' time, though it is also advisable for children and teens.
requirements: A facilitator who explains the value of the learning for performance or life quality at the outset of the learning experience
constraints: Most important for adult learners, especially in voluntary learning contexts with competing demands on adults' time; employers may still dictate learning in vocational settings (Day and Baskett)
target_learners: adult learners in voluntary adult education
target_learning_goals: motivation to learn; learner buy-in for required or elective adult learning
examples: The essay recommends addressing the learner's need to know from the beginning of the learning experience, drawing on Knowles' recommendation to make the intellectual case for learning's value
key_sources: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED507785

article_title: Pedagogy Is for Kids: Andragogy Is for Adults
citation: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults.
title: Use a transactional approach to methods, timing, and content with adult learners rather than assigning full responsibility to the teacher
description: The essay reports that Knowles "properly rejects the common pedagogical practice of assigning full responsibility to the teacher for methods, timing and content, and recommends a more transactional approach for andragogy." Under this approach, decisions about how, when, and what to learn are negotiated with learners rather than imposed, and the transactional approach should include addressing the learner's need to know from the beginning.
requirements: Willingness of the facilitator to share responsibility for methods, timing, and content decisions with adult learners
constraints: The essay frames this as most characteristic of andragogy with adults; children are described as more trusting of teachers and more likely to accept teacher-directed arrangements
target_learning_goals: learner motivation and ownership of the learning experience
examples: Knowles' recommendation, cited from his 1998 work (p. 72), that facilitators adopt a transactional rather than teacher-assigned approach
key_sources: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED507785

article_title: Deep Learning as an Individual, Conditional, and Contextual Influence on First-Year Student Outcomes
citation: Reason, R. D., Cox, B. E., McIntosh, K., & Terenzini, P. T. (2010). Deep learning as an individual, conditional, and contextual influence on first-year student outcomes. Paper presented at the Annual Forum of the Association for Institutional Research, Chicago, IL.
title: Do not expect environmental interventions alone to produce deep-learning benefits; students must personally engage in deep learning activities
description: Based on the finding that institutional aggregate DEEP scores predicted no outcomes while individual DEEP scores did, the authors conclude that "simply being a part of an environment in which deep learning is emphasized does not benefit students." Administrators designing environments to encourage deep processing should not expect a panacea effect, particularly for objective measures of learning; benefits require students' own effortful engagement in deep learning activities.
requirements: Students must personally put forth effort to engage in deep learning activities for benefits to accrue
constraints: The authors state the assumption that engagement is the mechanism through which deep processing affects learning needs further study
examples: The study found no significant relationship between institutions' average DEEP Learning scores and any of the four outcomes, while individual DEEP scores predicted all three self-reported gain scales
key_sources: Reason, R. D., Cox, B. E., McIntosh, K., & Terenzini, P. T. (2010). Deep learning as an individual, conditional, and contextual influence on first-year student outcomes. Paper presented at the Annual Forum of the Association for Institutional Research, Chicago, IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED520486

article_title: A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design
citation: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP
title: Two-step activity pattern: first develop a target motor-action scheme on a non-symbolic situated problem, then mathematize the scheme via interpolated semiotic means
description: The Kinemathics project choreographed a bimanual motor-action scheme enacting proportional equivalence and then engineered conditions for students to learn to move in a way that emulates it. The article's stated pattern is that 'Our two-step activity plan was for students to: (1) develop a target motor-action scheme as a dynamical solution to a situated problem bearing no mathematical symbolism; and (2) describe these schemes mathematically, using semiotic means we then interpolate into the action problem space.' This sequences embodied discovery before symbolic signification.
requirements: An embodied-interaction medium that gives favorable sensory feedback only under the target coordination, and semiotic artifacts (cursors, grid, numerals) available for later interpolation
constraints: The article treats the initial guided construction of operatory schemes more than their subsequent signification in disciplinary semiotic systems
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning grounded in sensorimotor coordination
examples: MIT-P stages: blank screen, then cursors, then a grid, then numerals along the y-axis, each introduced after a protocol criterion is satisfied
key_sources: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP

article_title: A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design
citation: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP
title: Treat all forms of instructional intervention — physical guidance, metaphoric framing, overlays — as productive constraints channeling the self-organizing learner–environment system
description: Drawing on ecological dynamics, the article proposes that instructors shape learning by channeling the self-organizing behavior of goal-oriented dynamical systems. It states that 'ecological dynamics regards all forms of intervention, such as physical guidance or metaphoric framing, as productive constraints on the solution of motor-action problems', with Newell's three constraint sources — organism, environment, and task — affecting behavior on short and long time scales. This gives STEM educational research interpretive schemes for modeling instructors' multimodal utterance and actions.
requirements: A goal-oriented motor-action problem whose solution space can be narrowed by manipulating organism, environment, or task constraints
constraints: The framework is offered for motor-action inquiry problems; the article notes institutional adoption would require rethinking teachers' professional practice from epistemology through assessment
target_learning_goals: construction of mathematically oriented operatory schemes
examples: The MIT-P facilitator's incremental overlay of cursors, grid, and numerals as environmental constraints on action
key_sources: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP

article_title: Speaking to Write: Examining Language Learners' Acceptance of Automatic Speech Recognition as a Writing Tool
citation: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327
title: Use ASR-based writing to lift the burden of error-free form so learners can attend to content and other aspects of writing
description: Because ESL students often focus on linguistic form at the expense of content, context, genre, and process, the article proposes ASR dictation as a way to redirect attention: "Using ASR, a technology that converts speech to text, may remove some of the burden of producing error-free form, allowing students to pay attention to other aspects of writing such as content." The tool is free, accessible, and meets Chapelle's CALL criteria, including attention to meaning and authentic use. The article frames this as pedagogically promising but not yet tested for effectiveness.
requirements: Training on the ASR tool before use
Learners' speech intelligible to the technology
constraints: Pedagogical effectiveness not yet assessed; the authors state studies are needed to determine its true pedagogical potential and best practices for classroom implementation
target_learners: adult ESL writers in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: attention to content, context, genre, and writing process rather than form alone
examples: Participants wrote authentic academic texts with ASR and reported focusing on getting the meaning of their ideas into texts without focusing on form
key_sources: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327

article_title: The Efficacy of Different Types of Metalinguistic Information in L2 Written Corrective Feedback
citation: Jang, Sung-Soo. (2020). The efficacy of different types of metalinguistic information in L2 written corrective feedback. English Teaching, 75(4), 33-56. https://doi.org/10.15858/engtea.75.4.202012.33
title: Pair written corrective feedback with immediate post-CF meaningful writing to convert explicit gains into implicit knowledge.
description: The article argues that written CF alone develops explicit knowledge, and that implicit knowledge develops only when learners immediately practice CF-targeted structures in a subsequent meaningful writing task. It states that "offering not only written CF but also subsequent opportunities for writing is required to develop learners' implicit knowledge beyond explicit knowledge", and that timely engagement was crucially responsible for the observed implicit gains.
requirements: A new piece of writing on CF-targeted structures must be carried out immediately after learners examine the written CF.
constraints: The contribution of post-CF writing for implicit knowledge may be restricted by its timing, per the immediacy finding the article cites from Chandler (2003).
target_learning_goals: Implicit knowledge of targeted grammatical structures (English article usage)
examples: In the experiment, the second dictogloss writing was carried out right after learners examined written CF on their first writing, and the DR, MS and MN groups showed implicit knowledge gains on the immediate posttest.
key_sources: Jang, Sung-Soo. (2020). The efficacy of different types of metalinguistic information in L2 written corrective feedback. English Teaching, 75(4), 33-56. https://doi.org/10.15858/engtea.75.4.202012.33

article_title: "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals
citation: Garrone-Shufran, S. (2022). "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals. Teacher Education Quarterly, Summer 2022.
title: ESL teacher education should explicitly teach systemic inequities and pair novices with advocacy mentors
description: Based on the finding that participants' advocacy was tactical and lacked attention to the why of advocacy, the article recommends that ESL teacher education coursework include explicit study of how school and societal systems reinforce stereotypes and disadvantage emergent bilinguals, and that programs create intentional mentorship pairings with experienced teachers who act as strong advocates. Mentors who enact advocacy in all spheres would be most desirable.
requirements: Mentors who can model advocacy for novice teachers
Coursework explicitly addressing advocacy and systemic inequities
constraints: The author notes one course alone was not clearly shown to change participants' thoughts and actions in long-lasting ways
target_learners: aspiring ESL teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: understanding systemic inequities affecting emergent bilinguals
examples: The author removed Suarez-Orozco et al. (2008) from the course and replaced it with three personal narratives by/about young adults who immigrated to the United States, to build empathy and awareness of systemic disadvantage
key_sources: Garrone-Shufran, S. (2022). "I Think You Have to Be a Fighter": Novice ESL Teachers' Descriptions of Advocacy for Emergent Bilinguals. Teacher Education Quarterly, Summer 2022. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1361502

article_title: Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review
citation: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137
title: Eight-strategy pattern for overcoming ESL pronunciation challenges within the CLT framework
description: The review proposes a matched set of eight strategies mirroring its eight identified challenges: a pronunciation-oriented curriculum within CLT, inclusion of pronunciation assessment, teacher preparedness through CPD, available pronunciation-integrated training, limited class size with longer class periods, technology-integrated pronunciation practice, availability of resources, and motivation among teachers and students. The review states "Implementing these strategies can significantly enhance the effectiveness of ESL pronunciation teaching in Bangladesh" and that a holistic approach combining them can improve students' communication skills.
requirements: Curriculum integration, regular assessment, targeted teacher training, technology use, and motivation, per the review's holistic approach
constraints: Strategies are proposed for the Bangladeshi secondary ESL context within the CLT framework
examples: The review's Figure 3 pairs each numbered challenge in Figure 2 with a corresponding numbered strategy
key_sources: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137

article_title: Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review
citation: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137
title: Improve ESL pronunciation through a holistic policy approach combining increased government budget, stakeholder negotiation, and accurate policy implementation
description: The review argues that improving ESL pronunciation within the CLT framework requires system-level action beyond the classroom: increased government budget allocations, negotiations among stakeholders, and accurate implementation of policies and practices. It states that "Increasing the budget dedicated to education, particularly for ESL programs, can facilitate the acquisition of modern educational technology, professional development for teachers, and the development of specialized pronunciation curriculum materials." It also calls for collaboration among government bodies, institutions, teachers, parents and the community, and for monitoring and evaluation mechanisms.
requirements: Sufficient financial resources; collaboration among government bodies, educational institutions, teachers, parents and the community; monitoring and evaluation mechanisms
constraints: The review frames this approach for the Bangladeshi ESL context within the CLT framework
examples: The review's discussion proposes language labs equipped with audio-visual aids, teacher engagement by policymakers, parental involvement at home, and collaboration with linguists and ESL experts to design pronunciation programs
key_sources: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137

article_title: Utilisation of SWOT Analysis for Decision-Making in Educational Contexts
citation: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219
title: Four-phase cyclical SWOT routine: diagnose, prioritise, implement, review and re-cycle
description: The CSM-SU organises strategic SWOT use into four interconnected, recurring phases: (1) Engage and Diagnose with multi-source internal and external data; (2) Interpret and Prioritise organisational interactions; (3) Develop and Implement actionable plans through distributed leadership; and (4) Review, Learn, and Re-Cycle insights. The updated SWOT profile "feeds directly back into Phase 1, triggering a new—and now more informed—cycle of diagnosis", embodying the feedback loops of open-systems theory. Each phase includes decision points allowing teams to customise activities to local circumstances.
requirements: Scheduled intervals at which the SWOT team reconvenes to review progress and update the SWOT profile
constraints: Schools vary in size, development stage, and community context, so phases must be adapted to local circumstances
target_learners: Teachers, support staff, parents, and students participating in strategic analysis
target_learning_goals: Strategic planning and adaptive school improvement
examples: Phase 1 combines quantitative data (achievement trends, attendance, budget) with qualitative sources (observations, interviews, climate indicators) and a simplified PEST scan to build a preliminary SWOT profile
key_sources: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219

article_title: Utilisation of SWOT Analysis for Decision-Making in Educational Contexts
citation: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219
title: Prioritise strategic actions by impact on learning and feasibility within existing capacity
description: To avoid initiative overload common in schools under multiple pressures, the CSM-SU's second phase assesses potential areas of action against two criteria: "impact on learning and improvement goals, and feasibility within existing capacity and resources". This disciplined prioritisation typically yields a focused set of three to five strategic priorities that are collectively constructed rather than imposed from above, increasing both decision quality and commitment to implementation.
requirements: Facilitated stakeholder workshops in which participants explore how strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats interact before prioritising
examples: The model guides leaders to narrow their focus to a small number of high-leverage, feasible priorities to support deeper implementation and mitigate fragmentation
key_sources: Keravnos, N., & Orphanos, S. (2025). Utilisation of SWOT analysis for decision-making in educational contexts. European Journal of Educational Management, 8(4), 219-234. https://doi.org/10.12973/eujem.8.4.219

article_title: Affordance-Based Approach to Language Assessment
citation: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000
title: Six analytic foci operationalize affordance dimensions as observable assessment lenses
description: The paper consolidates six vantage points as operational foci of affordance-based assessment: emergence, reciprocity, resonance, negotiation, disruption and reclamation, and latent trajectories. Each focus is a practical lens where multiple affordance dimensions intersect and become observable in classroom interaction, functioning as methodological bridges that render the five constitutive dimensions accessible for assessment. Each focus is defined, illustrated with a classroom vignette, and connected to ecological theory, with rubric levels and documentation mechanisms proposed for each.
requirements: Rubrics with qualitative descriptors, observation logs, digital artifacts, and learner reflections for documentation
constraints: Vignettes are demonstrative rather than systematic empirical data, given the paper's conceptual nature
target_learning_goals: documenting emergent, reciprocal, resonant, negotiated, resilient, and delayed engagement with learning opportunities
key_sources: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000

article_title: Affordance-Based Approach to Language Assessment
citation: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000
title: Affordance-based assessment should complement, not replace, outcome-based assessment
description: The paper explicitly states that an affordance perspective does not reject outcome-based assessments outright: standardized or outcome-oriented tasks remain useful for benchmarking and accountability. The affordance-based view instead reframes priorities, urging educators to look beyond test scores and consider how learners engage with and expand the opportunities before them, positioning assessment as both evaluative and generative.
requirements: Educators retain outcome-based tasks for benchmarking and accountability while adding ecological documentation
constraints: Affordance-based approaches risk inconsistency across cohorts, higher teacher workload, and difficulty ensuring reliability without a strong rubric and training
examples: Table 1 contrasts outcome-based methods such as a 90-minute closed-book end-of-term writing exam with affordance-based methods such as a semester-long portfolio of drafts, peer feedback, and self-reflection.
key_sources: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000

article_title: Are Learning Styles Relevant to Virtual Reality?
citation: Chwen Jen Chen, Seong Chong Toh, & Wan Mohd Fauzy Wan Ismail. (2005). Are Learning Styles Relevant To Virtual Reality? Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 38(2). https://www.iste.org
title: Provide VR-based learning environments with navigational aids to reduce extraneous cognitive load and improve learning outcomes
description: The article recommends designing VR learning environments with proper instructional support, specifically navigational aids such as a map tracer and directional arrows. It argues that "The eﬀorts to stay oriented when navigating through virtual environments take up mental resources" that would otherwise be available for understanding domain concepts, so aids supply the missing spatial-orientation schema and free resources for intrinsic load.
requirements: The learning problem requires learners to navigate within a virtual environment during learning
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one learning problem (beginning driver instruction) with intact classes and no pre-experimental sampling equivalence
target_learners: Form Four secondary students (approximately 16 years old) learning beginning driver instruction
target_learning_goals: Understanding of traffic rules and traffic signs in road scenarios
examples: The VR (guided exploration) mode provided "a tracer that provides a real-time indicator of the virtual vehicle position on a map, and directional arrows", and significantly outperformed the non-guided mode for both learning styles.
key_sources: Chwen Jen Chen, Seong Chong Toh, & Wan Mohd Fauzy Wan Ismail. (2005). Are Learning Styles Relevant To Virtual Reality? Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 38(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ728898

article_title: Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models
citation: Fore III, C., Boon, R. T., & Lowrie, K. (2007). Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 5(2), 49-73. https://www.ldworldwide.org
title: Teach content-area vocabulary to students with learning disabilities through explicit concept-model instruction rather than definition-only methods
description: Because students with learning disabilities acquire vocabulary poorly through independent word-learning strategies and definition lookup, the article recommends direct, explicit concept instruction: "the concept model, as a method of direct instruction, should be explicitly taught to students to facilitate independent word learning." The structured diagram format gives teachers and students a concrete outline of the word, its definition and characteristics, and examples and non-examples.
requirements: Direct and sequential teaching of target words, since students with LD take longer to learn new strategies
Words should be unfamiliar to most students (screened by a pretest of prior definitions)
constraints: Evidence base in this article is six seventh-graders with LD in one resource setting; the authors call for replication across more students, grade levels, content areas, and disability categories, and note maintenance and generalization were not measured
target_learning_goals: content-area vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension
examples: The study implemented the principle by replacing dictionary lookup and sentence writing with teacher-led concept-diagram lessons for mathematical terms
key_sources: Fore III, C., Boon, R. T., & Lowrie, K. (2007). Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 5(2), 49-73. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ797664

article_title: Comparing the Lecture-Based Learning With the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) Model of Learning in Enhancing the Skills of Consent-Taking in the Emergency Department: A Quasi-experimental Study.
citation: Khan Abdus Salam, Khan Muhammad Nasir Ayub, Khan Muhammad I. (2025). Comparing the Lecture-Based Learning With the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) Model of Learning in Enhancing the Skills of Consent-Taking in the Emergency Department: A Quasi-experimental Study. Cureus. https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.94133
title: Blend efficient lectures with structured 4C/ID-based workshops and role-play for consent-taking training
description: The article recommends that lectures continue to deliver foundational knowledge efficiently while being 'complemented by structured 4C/ID-based workshops and role-play to ensure meaningful skill transfer, engagement, and learner confidence'. It further urges emergency departments to integrate short, focused sessions into routine staff development and to make mixed physician–nurse group training standard practice to foster interprofessional collaboration.
requirements: Sessions must be deliverable without disrupting clinical operations, which the authors say the short, focused format allows
constraints: The lack of long-term follow-up limits conclusions regarding the sustainability of the observed improvements
The authors give this recommendation in the context of a small, single-center study
target_learning_goals: ethical communication in high-pressure clinical settings
examples: The study itself delivered a one-hour lecture to controls and a four-hour 4C/ID workshop with role-play to the intervention group, then assessed knowledge, OSCE skills, and perceptions.
key_sources: Khan Abdus Salam, Khan Muhammad Nasir Ayub, Khan Muhammad I. (2025). Comparing the Lecture-Based Learning With the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) Model of Learning in Enhancing the Skills of Consent-Taking in the Emergency Department: A Quasi-experimental Study. Cureus. https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.94133

article_title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
citation: Dickerson Broderick L., Gonzalez Drew E., Comfort Paul, Hardy John G., Hines Kelly E., Anderson Danielle N., Macaulay Timothy R., Stankovic Aleksandra, Twine Corey A. (2026). Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness. Frontiers in Physiology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2026.1950155
title: Integrate cognitive, physiological, behavioral, and operational metrics into mission-readiness monitoring
description: The review argues that no single monitoring stream captures mission readiness, so future monitoring systems should combine measurement streams. It states that "monitoring systems implemented in future LDS missions should integrate cognitive examinations with physiological, behavioral, and operational metrics to provide a comprehensive state of mission readiness". This includes wearable devices monitoring physiological stress responses, sleep, workload, and physical activity as adjunctive information, designed and ethically implemented to be operationally actionable.
requirements: Wearable and monitoring technologies must adhere to mission constraints and produce operationally actionable information
constraints: The review notes behavioral health monitoring is operationally difficult because interpersonal dynamics, stress, and mood are hard to quantify objectively, and astronauts may be reluctant to disclose stressors
target_learners: astronaut crews and mission-support teams across all mission phases
target_learning_goals: data-driven decision-making on physical and behavioral readiness
examples: The review describes wearable technology capable of monitoring heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, sleep patterns, workload, and physical activity
key_sources: Dickerson Broderick L., Gonzalez Drew E., Comfort Paul, Hardy John G., Hines Kelly E., Anderson Danielle N., Macaulay Timothy R., Stankovic Aleksandra, Twine Corey A. (2026). Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness.
